summary: Describes an architecture for creating and maintaining Service Function Chains, in which traffic passes through an ordered set of services. It covers concepts, principles and components, and does not propose protocols or solutions.

eli5.summary: Packages go along a conveyor belt past stations that each do a job, in a set order. This explains how to build such a belt.

questions: how does an sfc architecture work
what is the difference between an sfc and an sfp
what does a service function forwarder do
subtitle: The architecture for steering traffic through an ordered set of network services such as firewalls and NATs, independent of network topology.

tldr.problem: Service functions such as firewalls and NATs are deployed in relatively static ways, tied to network topology and physical resources, which makes it hard to introduce new services or build chains dynamically.
tldr.mechanism: Packets are classified on ingress, wrapped in an SFC encapsulation that identifies a Service Function Path, and forwarded by Service Function Forwarders through each service function in turn. Metadata can travel with the packets.
tldr.outcome: The RFC defines concepts, principles and components only. It does not propose protocols or solutions, and it applies to a single administrative domain.

facts.label: SFC encapsulation role
facts.value: Identifies the SFP; not used for packet forwarding

today: RFC 7665 is an Informational RFC and no later RFC is recorded as obsoleting or updating it. It describes the architecture only; the problem statement is in RFC 7498.

sections.title: Introduction and Scope
sections.content:
End-to-end services often need service functions (SFs): traditional ones such as firewalls and NATs, and application-specific ones. Defining an ordered set of them and steering traffic through them is Service Function Chaining (SFC). The problem statement is in RFC 7498.

The architecture is predicated on topological independence from the underlying forwarding topology. It is meant for a single network administrative domain, and inter-domain SFCs are left for future study. It applies to fixed and mobile networks and to data centers.

Its assumptions include that each SF is treated as an opaque processing element, that there is no global list of SFs or standard chaining logic, and that binding traffic to a chain is policy-based.
sections.eli5: Many networks bolt their helper boxes to fixed spots, so changing anything is a pain. This design lets you string the helpers together in any order you like.

sections.title: Chains, Paths and Rendered Paths
sections.content:
A Service Function Chain (SFC) is an ordered set of abstract service functions, for example a firewall, applied to traffic selected by classification. The order need not be linear: chains can branch, and a function can appear more than once, so cycles are possible. Chains can be unidirectional, bidirectional (a symmetric path using the same SF instances in both directions) or hybrid.

A Service Function Path (SFP) is the result of applying more detailed policy to a chain. It may name exact SFFs and SFs, or be vague and leave choices to the forwarder. One chain can have several paths; for example, one SFP may allow any order within Data Center 1 and another within Data Center 2.

The Rendered Service Path (RSP) is the actual sequence of SFFs and SFs a packet visits. So chain, path and rendered path are progressive refinements: a chain asking for a firewall and a caching engine, a path choosing a data center, and a rendered path choosing exact instances.
sections.eli5: A chain is the recipe: first wash, then peel, then chop. A path says which kitchen to use. The rendered path is exactly which cook did each step today.

sections.title: Principles and Components
sections.content:
The RFC lists key principles: topological independence, plane separation (building paths is separate from forwarding packets), classification, shared metadata, service definition independence, service function chain independence, and heterogeneous control and policy points.

The main logical components are:

  • Classifier: matches traffic against policy at the ingress of the domain and attaches it to an SFP. Reclassification later in a path can select a new SFP, which is called branching.
  • SFC encapsulation: identifies the SFP and can carry metadata. It is not a transport encapsulation and is not used to forward packets across the network, so any network transport can carry it.
  • Service Function Forwarder (SFF): uses the encapsulation to forward packets to attached SFs, passes them on to the next SFF, and terminates the path by removing the encapsulation after the last SF.
  • Service Function: may be SFC-aware or SFC-unaware.
  • SFC proxy: strips and re-applies the SFC encapsulation on behalf of an SFC-unaware SF, so the SFF sees it as an SFC-aware SF.

SFC boundary nodes handle the edges: an ingress node adds the encapsulation, and an egress node must remove SFC-specific information, including any sensitive data.
sections.eli5: A sorting desk at the door decides which conveyor line a package gets. A label on the box says which line. Helpers along the line read the label, do their job and pass it on. Old helpers who cannot read labels get a translator at their side.

sections.title: Metadata, Control and Operations
sections.content:
Shared metadata lets classifiers, SFs and external systems exchange context along a path. For example, a classifier can add subscriber information obtained from an external repository so that SFs can use it for local policy. Some SFCs need no metadata at all.

The SFC control plane builds SFPs, translates chains into forwarding paths and distributes the information, and may be distributed or centralized. Policy decides which SFs are available and which sequences are valid, and is kept separate from the data plane. The detailed control plane is out of scope.

Other concerns the RFC says solutions must address:

  • Loops: limited, policy-compliant loops must be permitted, but solutions must prevent infinite service function loops.
  • Load balancing: elastic functions should not need separate chains, and where an SF is reachable through several SFFs, exactly one SFF must take responsibility for it. An SFF must keep all packets of a flow handled the same way because an SF may be stateful.
  • MTU: encapsulation and transport headers enlarge packets, and fragmenting inside an SFF would be a major processing increase.
  • OAM: both in-band, sharing the path and fate of user packets, and out-of-band.
  • Resilience: responding quickly to failed links, SFFs or SFs. Per-SF state is the SF's responsibility.
sections.eli5: The belt can carry sticky notes about each package. Also, a belt must not loop forever, boxes must not get squashed by extra wrapping, and someone must check that the belt still works.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Moving from static, topology-dependent deployment to chaining can change how data flows, so security and privacy must be reevaluated. The RFC groups concerns into four areas: the service overlay, the boundaries of the domain, classification, and the SFC encapsulation.

At the boundary, transport mechanisms MUST ensure that outside parties cannot inject SFC packets that will be accepted for processing, including through tunnels to other domains. Metadata may be sensitive or reveal personally identifying information, and realizations MUST protect it. Where control systems know such data may be added, they MUST verify that protective treatment is available from where it is added to where it is removed, and SHOULD generate error notifications if it is not.
sections.eli5: Only people inside the factory may put boxes on the belt, and any private notes stuck to boxes must be kept safe. If the safe-keeping is missing, someone should be told.
